W4_holm.procedure: Holm step-down, family of 7 arms-vs-no-rescoring tests, alpha=0.05. Step 1: Jev p=0.006 <= 0.05/7=0.0071 -> reject. Step 2: OPT-6.7b p=0.035 > 0.05/6=0.0083 -> stop.

recompute_attempt.method: paired bootstrap, 5000 resamples, test split only (978 sents), each per-candidate arm at its recorded tuned alpha, one-sided for improvement
recompute_attempt.why_not_used: Clean-room recompute used a standard word-level Levenshtein WER that reproduces every top-1 selection exactly (first-pass sentence accuracy 68.003% = reported 68.0029%) but yields systematically larger arm-vs-baseline WER deltas (e.g. OPT -0.66pp vs reported -0.29pp), hence much smaller p-values. The paper's exact WER normalization could not be recovered (tested: jiwer, stemming, mean-of-ratios, concatenated-corpus, dedup, split variants). Jev's typed pick is not recoverable from the cached per-candidate scores (best reproduction reaches 69.9% test sentence accuracy vs reported 71.3%), so no recompute was possible. Holm was therefore applied to the reported p-values.

W8_alpha_stability.method: 200 seeded bootstrap resamples of the 419-sentence dev set; alpha refit on 0.00-1.00 grid step 0.05 per resample (ties -> smallest alpha); test WER of each refit alpha on the 978-sentence test set. WER via the clean-room word-Levenshtein implementation (see W4 note); point refits land one grid step from recorded alphas, consistent with a flat optimum.
W8_alpha_stability.grid_verified: 0.00 to 1.00 step 0.05; full-dev refits: opt 0.25 (rec 0.30), qwen 0.50 (rec 0.45), gpt2 0.30 (rec 0.25), gpt2medium 0.15 (rec 0.20), gpt2small 0.00 (rec 0.40), distilgpt2 0.00 (rec 0.20)
W8_alpha_stability.conclusion: Chosen alpha is unstable across dev resamples (std 0.10-0.16, spread over ~10 grid values per arm) but the resulting test WER is stable (std 0.10-0.21pp; e.g. opt 8.88 +/- 0.21, range 8.68-9.39). Tuning on 419 sentences does not overfit in the sense that matters: the WER surface is flat near the optimum, so alpha jitter barely moves test WER.

b_global_vs_perlist.method: Global variant: single mean/std per score type estimated on DEV lists only (no test leakage), applied to dev (alpha retuned on 0.05 grid) and test. Per-list variant at recorded alphas. WER via clean-room implementation; comparison is relative so the recipe offset cancels.
b_global_vs_perlist.conclusion: Global normalization is strictly worse for every arm (+0.08 to +0.42pp test WER) and collapses the retuned alpha to 0.00-0.05: a single global std cannot align LM log-likelihoods whose scale varies wildly across lists, so dev tuning discards the LM entirely (4 of 6 arms choose alpha=0). Per-list z-normalization is load-bearing for rescoring; the arm ranking shuffles (OPT becomes best) but no new significance claim emerges under the global variant.

c_short_lists.conclusion: No pathology: on <10-candidate lists the per-list z-norm top-1 agrees with a raw-score combination on 99.5% of lists, and short-list WER is ~0.5% under either rule (short lists are easy). Single-candidate lists are safe (z=0 -> the only candidate is picked); std=0 is guarded.

a_isotonic.method: IsotonicRegression fit on DEV (x = top-1 max-softmax-prob at T=0.25, y = sentence correctness), applied to test; coverage-risk recomputed.
a_isotonic.inversions: 0 of 477753 sentence pairs reversed (isotonic only merges adjacent ranks into ties, never inverts)
a_isotonic.conclusion: Ranking verified unchanged empirically, as theory requires. Pure recalibration cannot move the coverage-risk curve: the gap to Jev is not a calibration problem.

b_signals.method: Per-sentence signals on dev->test at recorded T=0.25 and tuned alphas, on the clean-room pipeline (paper's exact abstention top-1 picks not reproducible, see W4 note; 100%-coverage points: mine 31.49/32.41 vs recorded 28.43/28.73). Curves are sentence-error % at 30/50/70/90/100% coverage.
b_signals.conclusion: Max-softmax-prob (the current baseline) is the best per-candidate ranking signal; the top1-top2 margin is second; the raw top-1 combined score is anti-informative (error rises as coverage falls: per-list z-scoring makes raw top-1 values incomparable across lists). No per-candidate signal choice closes the gap: the baseline already uses the best one.

Q7_abstention.calibration_vs_ranking: Decisive evidence comes from the recorded curves themselves: at 100% coverage OPT (28.4%) and Jev (28.7%) have identical top-1 sentence error, yet Jev's curve falls far faster (30% coverage: 3.4% vs 7.5%). Same accuracy, better ordering of kept sentences => Jev's abstention advantage is a RANKING advantage (its confidences separate correct from incorrect sentences: conf_right/conf_wrong 0.736/0.409, gap 0.327, vs OPT 0.647/0.368, gap 0.279), not calibration and not top-1 accuracy. Isotonic recalibration provably cannot recover such a gap.
